newsitem.title: USA: Stingy Buba to drag heels on way to EMU - US experts.
newsitem.headline: Stingy Buba to drag heels on way to EMU - US experts.

text.p: The Bundesbank, still haunted by having little say before the two German marks were merged in 1990, will eschew lowering official interest rates merely to abet the German government's push to create a single European currency, U.S. experts said.
"They don't want to pay the price for a single currency like they did for German unification," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, a market consulting firm.

Moreover, economists said the German central bank seems unconvinced another dose of monetary easing will cure Germany's economic problems and may fear a rate cut could have an undesireable effect on long-term German borrowing costs.

With key interest rates already at post-World War II lows, the Bundesbank has said there is already enough easing in the pipeline. What is preventing the economy from responding are structural problems related to the labor market, over which it has little control, market economists pointed out.
"The Bundesbank will influence the process a little bit more by being stingy on interest rates and not acquiescing in the political push that (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl is spearheading," Gilmore said.

After the 1989 collapse of the Berlin Wall, the central bank cautioned against the likely costs of West Germany's hazardously generous offer to fuse the German currencies at a one-for-one exchange rate. Its enjoinders went unheeded, and the consequences were measured largely in terms of much higher German interest rates.

The Bundesbank was forced to maintain a very restrictive monetary policy for several years following reunification to counter the inflationary effects of diluting the new German currency with an overvalued ostmark.

Once again the central bank finds itself fighting to have a voice in what is essentially a political process. It certainly has no interest in setting in place the kind of monetary stimulus that will lead to a weak euro, economists said.

"Decisions are being made outside of the ambit of the Bundesbank and they are certainly not going to lay down and continue to stimulate aggressively to effect a process about which they are very dubious," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc in Chicago.
But this does not rule out the Bundesbank reluctantly loosening credit for purely domestic economic reasons, economists said.
Germany's sluggish economic rebound sputtered in the fourth quarter of 1996, with economic output declining 0.2 percent, according to the Bundesbank's own data.

As the economy ran out of steam, the chances of generating sufficient government revenues to meet a key condition for joining the single currency planned for 1999 -- a budget deficit not exceeding 3.0 percent of gross domestic product -- seemed to recede.

Even more alarming, German unemployment swelled to depression-era levels in January, showing that 4.7 million Germans were without work. The unemployment rate advanced to 12.2 percent, a condition Germans are increasingly blaming on government budget slashing before European Economic and Monetary Union.
Rothfield said that changes in Germany's securities repurchase (repo) rate -- the rate the Bundesbank sets for overnight loans between banks -- are closely correlated to Germany's employment data.
"The econometric work we do indicates that changes in Germany's repo rate are most closely related to quarterly changes in German employment, more than anything else.
"I still see them cutting, but it is in spite of monetary union not because of it," Rothfield said.
But the repo rate, which the Bundesbank has held at 3.0 percent since August, is not as significant for the markets as the German discount rate, economists said.
They are doubtful the Buba will push the discount rate below its current 2.5 percent and recent comments by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer seem to confirm this view.

In a radio interview last week, Tietmeyer said with German central bank and capital market interest rates at record lows, the preconditions for new growth are given and another cut in interest rates is not likely in the short term.

Furthermore, with German inflation running at 1.5 to 2.0 percent, the inflation cushion is relatively thin already and a rate cut by the usually hyper-vigilant Bundesbank might scare off German bond holders, which would increase borrowing costs and further restrict economic growth, analysts said.

"When the Bundesbank says they have made their contribution to easing the cyclical problems in Germany, that is a reasonable statement," said Anne Parker Mills, foreign exchange analyst at Lehman Brothers.

"At this point a sharp cut in interest rates could be counterproductive. What they would like to happen is for long- term rates to come down and were they to cut short rates that could have a perverse impact at long end of the curve," she added.
The Bundesbank council next meets to consider interest rates on Thursday March 6.
